item.title: PostgreSQL patches 52 security holes, sends version 14 into retirement
item.description: PostgreSQL developers have patched 52 security vulnerabilities and more than 140 bugs in updates spanning versions 14 to 18, alongside a second release candidate for version 19. The batch includes PostgreSQL 14.25, the final release for the now-unsupported version 14. Users are advised to move to a newer major version. Some fixes also require follow-up work, including rebuilding affected indexes or taking a fresh full backup. Administrators should check the release's post-update instructions. Alastair Turner, community technologist at open source consultancy Percona, said the high-severity code execution flaws should be taken seriously, although exploiting them requires database access. "This isn't something just a brute-force scan of the right port is going to find," he said. "They can make compromises through SQL injection or credential theft a lot worse, but don't create the opportunity for remote, anonymous code execution." Among the fixes is CVE-2026-6460 , a type confusion flaw that could let a database user with permission to create objects execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.8 out of 10. Turner attributed the growing number of security discoveries partly to AI-assisted scanning and partly to increased scrutiny as PostgreSQL gains ground in enterprise computing. "It is a record number of CVEs fixed in a quarterly release, and I don't think we've seen the end of that trend. Looking down the list of where these CVEs came from, we see Anthropic and OpenAI open source scanners, so it is clear AI or brute force is playing a role," he said. Turner said the fixes spanned multiple parts of the software. There "isn't one piece of code that was broken" but rather "a wide base that got patched." "It's also worth noting that this is the third quarterly release in a row which sets a new record for the number of CVEs patched," he added. PostgreSQL 14 users now face a major-version upgrade or running without further security and bug fixes. Their destination may depend on internal upgrade policies. Organizations that require the previous major release, known as N-1, would currently target PostgreSQL 17, Turner noted. Version 18 remains the latest generally available release until 19 arrives. PostgreSQL 19 is scheduled for general availability on Thursday, November 19, barring further problems. It is set to include a new REPACK command , whose CONCURRENTLY option allows reads and writes to continue while disk space is reclaimed. VACUUM FULL requires an exclusive table lock, blocking reads and writes while it runs. ®

item.title: Declan Rice agrees new Arsenal contract making him club’s joint highest-paid player
item.description: Deal will run to 2031 and worth about £300,000 a week Jurriën Timber also agrees fresh contract extension Declan Rice has agreed a new five-year contract at Arsenal, with the England midfielder poised to match Bukayo Saka’s status as the highest-paid player at the Premier League champions. Representatives for Rice, who won his 82nd cap in England’s thrilling win over Spain on Sunday, have been in talks for months about extending the deal he signed in 2023 after a record £105m move from West Ham. That is believed to be worth about £250,000 a week and is due to expire in 2028, although Arsenal have the option of a further 12 months. Continue reading...

item.title: Are Nigerian Artists Dominating the Grammys’ Best African Music Performance Category?
item.description: Tems receiving the Best African Music Performance at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards. In June 2023, ahead of the 66th Grammy Awards, the Recording Academy announced the creation of the Best African Music Performance category. Its creation was a recognition of how far African music had travelled globally, and Nigerian artists were at the centre of that movement. From Burna Boy ‘s Ye , CKay ‘s Love Nwantiti , Wizkid ‘s explosive Essence , to Rema ‘s globally successful Calm Down and others, Nigerian artists became drivers of African music’s global expansion. Afrobeats – the umbrella term often used internationally to describe much of contemporary African popular music, although many Nigerian artists have rejected it for its tendency to limit the range of music coming out of the country – became an established genre globally. While Nigerian and African music have always travelled beyond their respective countries, the era of streaming and digital platforms has accelerated how quickly global audiences discover and engage with the music. African music became increasingly established in the West and other parts of the world, creating greater recognition for its artists and sounds. The Grammys’ decision to introduce a category specifically recognising African music performances was an important step in that direction, beyond the recognition African artists had previously received in categories such as Best Global Music Album. Although the creation of the Best African Music Performance category was celebrated throughout the continent, there seems to be a monopoly, or something close to it, of Nigerian music in the category. While South African artist Tyla has won the award twice, more than any individual Nigerian artist, Nigerian artists have consistently enjoyed greater representation in the nominations. Indeed, Nigerian artists are considerably more recognised globally, particularly in the West. However, I believe it is the responsibility of an award of this repute to look beyond the most visible names and recognise the best African music released within its eligibility period. A song should not earn a nomination simply because it is popular or has enjoyed international success. A closer look at the nominations across the four editions reveals just how much Nigerian music has featured in the category. In 2024, four of the five nominated recordings featured Nigerian artists. The following year, all five recordings had Nigerian representation, with seven Nigerian artists making the list. In 2026, three of the five recordings featured Nigerian artists, while the 2027 nominations saw four out of five recordings feature at least one Nigerian artist. Altogether, Nigerian artists have featured in 16 of the 20 nominated recordings since the category was introduced. This is not to suggest that Nigerian music does not deserve the recognition it receives. Nigerian artists have built impressive international careers, and their music has found audiences far beyond th

Its creation was a recognition of how far African music had travelled globally, and Nigerian artists were at the centre of that movement. From Burna Boy ‘s Ye , CKay ‘s Love Nwantiti , Wizkid ‘s explosive Essence , to Rema ‘s globally successful Calm Down and others, Nigerian artists became drivers of African music’s global expansion. Afrobeats – the umbrella term often used internationally to describe much of contemporary African popular music, although many Nigerian artists have rejected it for its tendency to limit the range of music coming out of the country – became an established genre globally. While Nigerian and African music have always travelled beyond their respective countries, the era of streaming and digital platforms has accelerated how quickly global audiences discover and engage with the music. African music became increasingly established in the West and other parts of the world, creating greater recognition for its artists and sounds. The Grammys’ decision to introduce a category specifically recognising African music performances was an important step in that direction, beyond the recognition African artists had previously received in categories such as Best Global Music Album. Although the creation of the Best African Music Performance category was celebrated throughout the continent, there seems to be a monopoly, or something close to it, of Nigerian music in the category. While South African artist Tyla has won the award twice, more than any individual Nigerian artist, Nigerian artists have consistently enjoyed greater representation in the nominations. Indeed, Nigerian artists are considerably more recognised globally, particularly in the West. However, I believe it is the responsibility of an award of this repute to look beyond the most visible names and recognise the best African music released within its eligibility period. A song should not earn a nomination simply because it is popular or has enjoyed international success. A closer look at the nominations across the four editions reveals just how much Nigerian music has featured in the category. In 2024, four of the five nominated recordings featured Nigerian artists. The following year, all five recordings had Nigerian representation, with seven Nigerian artists making the list. In 2026, three of the five recordings featured Nigerian artists, while the 2027 nominations saw four out of five recordings feature at least one Nigerian artist. Altogether, Nigerian artists have featured in 16 of the 20 nominated recordings since the category was introduced. This is not to suggest that Nigerian music does not deserve the recognition it receives. Nigerian artists have built impressive international careers, and their music has found audiences far beyond the continent. They deserve to be recognised. However, when a category is created to recognise the best of African music, it is worth asking how much of the continent’s musical diversity is reflected in its nominations. In September 2024, Tyla made a similar observation when she won the Best Afrobeats award at the MTV Video Music Awards. In her acceptance speech, she said, “There is a tendency to group all African artists under Afrobeats… Even though Afrobeats has run things and has opened so many doors for us, African music is so diverse. It is more than just Afrobeats.” Africa has a vast and diverse music industry. From South Africa’s Amapiano movement and Ghana’s Highlife and Hiplife traditions to Uganda’s dance music, Tanzania’s Bongo Flava and the different sounds emerging from Francophone Africa, there is no shortage of music deserving of international attention. The prominence of Nigerian artists in this category may partly reflect the strength of the country’s music industry and the international visibility its artists have built over the years. It may also reflect the Recording Academy’s membership, voting processes and the music that reaches its voters. But that is precisely why the conversation is important. If the category is to represent African music, its nominations should encourage listeners to discover artists and sounds beyond the ones they already know. Nigerian music has benefited from a relatively strong music industry, with established record labels, international distribution deals, collaborations with global artists and a large diaspora audience that continues to support its exports. These factors have helped Nigerian artists reach international audiences and, by extension, become more visible to institutions such as the Recording Academy. However, this visibility does not necessarily mean that the best or most interesting music coming out of Africa is always the music that gets heard internationally. An artist from another African country may be producing equally compelling music but lack the distribution network, marketing resources or international connections to get it beyond their local market. If the music awards are interested in recognising the best of African music, perhaps there is also a need to look beyond the music that already has an established international audience. After all, one of the things an award can do is introduce the world to music it might otherwise never discover. There is a difference between recognising the best of African music and repeatedly recognising only the most internationally visible parts of it. The Best African Music Performance has opened an important door for African music. The next step is ensuring that more of the continent gets to walk through it. The post Are Nigerian Artists Dominating the Grammys’ Best African Music Performance Category? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation
item.description: For the last decade, the datacenter industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy. It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity. They are becoming active participants in energy generation, storage, and grid management through behind-the-meter infrastructure. This is being driven by the explosive rise of AI and a manufacturing renaissance. Power demand is growing again, increasing an average of 2.1 percent annually over the past five years, with datacenters emerging as a dominant driver of long-term growth. Electric Power Research Institute projects that datacenters could consume as much as 17 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030 , more than triple their current 4-5 percent share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid. Key regional utility transmission organizations are expected to face critical reserve shortfalls as early as 2028. At the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of new generation and storage capacity was represented by projects actively seeking interconnection to the U.S. grid. For the projects that successfully reached commercial operation, the process took a median of more than five years from request to completion. To keep building at the speed of innovation, datacenter operators are fundamentally rethinking their relationship with power , shifting from being passive grid consumers to active, localized energy producers. Grid capacity is no longer the ceiling. Instead, the next chapter of digital infrastructure will be written behind the meter. Behind-the-meter (BTM) refers to energy assets located on the customer side of the utility connection, including battery systems, microgrids, generators, fuel cells, and distributed energy resources that can operate independently of grid constraints. item.dc:creator: Steve Carlini
item.content:encoded: For the last decade, the datacenter industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy. It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity. They are becoming active participants in energy generation, storage, and grid management through behind-the-meter infrastructure. This is being driven by the explosive rise of AI and a manufacturing renaissance. Power demand is growing again, increasing an average of 2.1 percent annually over the past five years, with datacenters emerging as a dominant driver of long-term growth. Electric Power Research Institute projects that datacenters could consume as much as 17 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030 , more than triple their current 4-5 percent share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid. Key regional utility transmission organizations are expected to face critical reserve shortfalls as early as 2028. At the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of new generation and storage capacity was represented by projects actively seeking interconnection to the U.S. grid. For the projects that successfully reached commercial operation, the process took a median of more than five years from request to completion. To keep building at the speed of innovation, datacenter operators are fundamentally rethinking their relationship with power , shifting from being passive grid consumers to active, localized energy producers. Grid capacity is no longer the ceiling. Instead, the next chapter of digital infrastructure will be written behind the meter. Behind-the-meter (BTM) refers to energy assets located on the customer side of the utility connection, including battery systems, microgrids, generators, fuel cells, and distributed energy resources that can operate independently of grid constraints. The Role of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) While every datacenter developer faces grid constraints, the industry’s two dominant business models are adopting distinctly different strategies to bypass the power bottleneck. Hyperscale Operators Hyperscale operators (tech giants like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) utilize their massive balance sheets to secure gigawatt-scale capacity directly. Rather than acting as passive grid customers, hyperscalers are taking direct, active control of their energy supply chains. They negotiate custom, state-level tariffs directly with utilities, co-locate facilities next to large nuclear or baseload assets, and sign massive off-site Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Increasingly, hyperscalers are also deploying large-scale, on-site Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to bypass grid delays and accelerate their projects. Many are also turning to behind-the-meter natural gas generation to provide additional power on-site. With larger, hundreds-of-megawatts turbines facing long backlogs, some operators are instead deploying multiple smaller, roughly 50 MW turbines in parallel, either on-site or adjacent to the campus. Colocation Providers In contrast, colocation (colo) providers lease space, power, and cooling to third-party tenants. Colos operate on a highly competitive, faster-to-market model where speed-to-revenue is the primary metric. Colocation facilities are geographically constrained, as their facilities must be located close to business hubs to minimize latency rather than simply next to remote power plants. Consequently, datacenter and colocation developers are increasingly integrating on-site, behind-the-meter energy solutions. In highly congested markets, BTM generation and battery storage can provide a path to power while developers wait for grid interconnection. In Virginia, for example, LS Power is pursuing a 300 MW datacenter project designed to receive power directly from its adjacent natural gas-fired Doswell power plant, creating a behind-the-meter supply arrangement that can help accelerate access to power. At the same time, the rules for connecting large loads are beginning to change. In some U.S. markets, datacenters that can provide flexible load, on-site generation or storage are gaining new pathways to connect while giving grid operators greater control over demand during periods of constraint. The New Coordinated Energy Stack: UPS + BESS + Generators Historically, a datacenter’s power architecture was passive, consisting of an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to bridge 5-to-15 minutes of downtime and backup diesel generators to handle prolonged outages. AI has shattered this legacy design. Although many enterprise deployments still operate below 20 kW per rack, next-generation AI clusters are increasingly exceeding 100 kW per rack, with some designs targeting significantly higher densities. Furthermore, AI training runs create highly volatile, synchronized compute loads, causing electricity draw to spike and drop in massive, sub-second waves. To protect both sensitive computing equipment and the local grid from these fluctuations, operators are deploying a layered, grid-interactive energy stack: UPS (Instant Protection): Positioned in series with the servers, the traditional UPS remains essential for providing millisecond-fast power conditioning and preventing data loss during transient voltage sags. BESS (On-site Shock Absorber & Optimizer): Connected in parallel at the facility level, BESS acts as a real-time shock absorber. It smooths out volatile AI compute spikes, stores cost-effective off-peak power for use during peak hours, and participates in grid-balancing services. On-site Generation (Long-Term Firm Power): Customer-sited generation, including natural gas microturbines, provides the ultimate firm baseload capacity, insulating the facility from grid failures for days or weeks. By layering these technologies, operators can stop treating their power systems like a pricey “insurance policy” that sits idle, and start using them as a smart, money-saving asset. In many markets, demand charges (the fees utilities charge based on peak power draw) make up 30-to-70 percent of a datacenter’s monthly electricity bill. By discharging on-site batteries during peak demand periods — a strategy known as peak shaving — operators can reduce the peak loads used to calculate demand charges, potentially lowering electricity costs significantly. Turning Backup Assets into Strategic Grid Partners Historically, backup diesel generators sat untouched, accumulating maintenance costs unless a blackout occurred. Today, utilities and datacenter operators are establishing mutually beneficial partnerships. Through Virtual Power Plants (VPPs), utilities can aggregate a datacenter’s distributed backup generators and BESS capacity into a single, software-controlled resource. Under grid stress, the utility can dispatch these on-site assets, effectively turning the datacenter into a power supplier rather than a power drain. A prime example is Google’s three-year partnership with Voltus, which will aggregate up to 100 MW of flexible distributed energy resources across the PJM footprint, the regional transmission organization that coordinates electricity supply and demand across 13 states and the District of Columbia. The effort is designed to support grid reliability and help unlock capacity for datacenter growth. In some regions, regulators are increasingly requiring large energy users to build flexibility into how they operate. For example, in Texas, Senate Bill 6 establishes new requirements for large loads of 75 MW or more, including the ability to curtail grid consumption during energy emergencies. For datacenters, meeting those requirements will depend on flexible workloads, on-site generation, and battery energy storage that can help maintain critical operations while reducing grid demand. Crucially, incorporating BESS into this stack minimizes the environmental impact of these curtailment events. Instead of firing up diesel generators for a brief 10-minute gri

item.title: Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
item.description: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. Continue reading...

item.title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
item.description: Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February , but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”. Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head. Continue reading...

item.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
item.description: New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients. But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market . Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each. Continue reading...

item.title: Fifa accused of climate ‘record of failure’ due to Aramco deal and tournament expansion
item.description: Groups question ‘sincerity’ to meet emissions pledges Oil giant is a major sponsor of football governing body The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action. Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”. Continue reading...

item.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
item.description: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds , telcos , retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®

According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds , telcos , retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®

item.title: 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer
item.description: Indian tech giant Tata Consultancy Services has a new client, iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse which has made a third of its IT department redundant. Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error. We hear from staff that the botched invitation was taken as a clue of what was to happen next, namely the announcement of 230 redundancies plus an end to 120 contracted roles. The town hall meeting was not interactive, with a Bunnings rep speaking from a script and not taking questions. Staff whose roles will end then received an email inviting them to a meeting. Bunnings, whose logo is a hammer, has tried to explain the decision in a statement that says, “We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us.” “These changes reflect the way customers are choosing to shop and the increasingly competitive retail environment,” the statement adds, before pointing out “Bunnings is already investing in technology and digital experiences to respond to these changes, earlier this year becoming the first Australian retailer to launch an AI-powered shopping agent using Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience platform through Buddy.” Some of the TCS workers Bunnings is hiring will work in Australia. Others will work from India and the Philippines. While Bunnings follows the template of a big box retailer, each of its stores allows charities and community groups to run fundraising barbeques in its forecourt every weekend. Those barbeques are a significant source of income for many non-profits and have earned the chain a broad social license. The hardware barn is so well-known that children’s TV show Bluey – the most viewed program of 2024 and 2025 in the US – gently parodied it as "Hammerbarn" it in an episode. The Register mentions this because we understand the reference to TCS staff helping to deliver the Bunnings experience has gone down badly, as the chain’s employees wonder how offshore workers who have not experienced its stores and atmosphere can deliver a service that preserves its culture. Bunnings says its new IT operating model will commence in July 2027 and that “Impacted team members will be supported in their roles through Christmas, with any changes taking effect in the new year.” The company’s IT team will still employ around 500 people. These job losses add to a rotten year for Australia’s tech scene, which this year saw local heroes Canva and Atlassian farewell hundreds of staff. Iconic Australian airline Qantas last week outsourced hundreds of jobs to India through Accenture. ®

item.title: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China
item.description: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations. The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities. US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers. No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import. Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers. Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators. “Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.” He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.” “Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.” Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its
item.dc:creator: Simon Sharwood
item.content:encoded: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations. The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities. US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers. No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import. Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers. Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators. “Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.” He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.” “Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.” Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China. It remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub. Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers. Interestingly, the new BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.” Chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ® UDPATED AT 05:45 UTC, November 17 to add news that late on Monday the US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Megaspeed. In the announcement, the two departments detail investigative activities they conducted across 2024 and 2025, including a June meeting with Alice Huang in Singapore, and state those details "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." Singaporean authorities have also said that meeting took place, but say they asked asked US counterparts for help with their own investigations and received frustratingly little support. Singapore also investigated Supermicro's possible role at Megapseed, and complained that the server-maker didn't co-operate either. Supermicro today told The Register it " does not conduct business with these entities" and operates a "robust compliance program." "We are committed to complying with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws and regulations, and we require our distributors and resellers to do the same," according to a Supermicro statement sent to The Register .

item.title: California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety
item.description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI under the state's unfair competition and public nuisance laws, for allegedly misleading and endangering the public by deploying unsafe AI models. The lawsuit [PDF], filed in California Superior Court, follows the compromise of Hugging Face's infrastructure and other cyber incidents OpenAI's experimental models caused when taking autonomous actions without authorization or supervision. "While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," said Attorney General Bonta. At a press conference , Bonta added: "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public." The legal salvo comes after Bonta in September sent OpenAI a letter seeking information about these agentic attacks. According to the complaint, "OpenAI failed to substantially comply" with the investigatory subpoena. In August, 15 states led by Iowa – and excluding California – issued a joint demand for OpenAI to provide information about how its models hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. Bonta's office previously joined with Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings to urge OpenAI to do more for children's safety in light of reports that its models produced sexually inappropriate output. California did not, however, join the eight states that sued OpenAI in October over alleged misrepresentations about child safety. Florida and Texas have also made child safety claims. Child safety plays well politically; California appears to be the first state to demand more accountability toward the general public. Bonta's lawsuit, in a state that has largely accommodated the AI industry for the sake of economic benefits and political contributions , suggests that California officials may be more willing to bite the hand that feeds. The many Democratic victories in the US midterm elections may also be a factor, as pundits feel voters swung to give lawmakers license to regulate the unpopular AI industry. At his press conference, Bonta made sure to convey that he wants accountability without smothering the AI industry in costly regulation. "Let me be clear," he said. "I believe in the technological and economic power of AI. If we're able to address these very high stakes safety issues, AI could lead to some of the most incredible improvements in the history of humankind." AI is yet to deliver those incredible improvements. It has delivered deepfakes, huge quantities of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the permissionless resale of past intellectual labor, plus high energy and RAM prices. As well as some productivity gains

At a press conference , Bonta added: "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public." According to the complaint, "OpenAI failed to substantially comply" with the investigatory subpoena. In August, 15 states led by Iowa – and excluding California – issued a joint demand for OpenAI to provide information about how its models hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. Bonta's office previously joined with Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings to urge OpenAI to do more for children's safety in light of reports that its models produced sexually inappropriate output. California did not, however, join the eight states that sued OpenAI in October over alleged misrepresentations about child safety. Florida and Texas have also made child safety claims. Child safety plays well politically; California appears to be the first state to demand more accountability toward the general public. Bonta's lawsuit, in a state that has largely accommodated the AI industry for the sake of economic benefits and political contributions , suggests that California officials may be more willing to bite the hand that feeds. The many Democratic victories in the US midterm elections may also be a factor, as pundits feel voters swung to give lawmakers license to regulate the unpopular AI industry. At his press conference, Bonta made sure to convey that he wants accountability without smothering the AI industry in costly regulation. "Let me be clear," he said. "I believe in the technological and economic power of AI. If we're able to address these very high stakes safety issues, AI could lead to some of the most incredible improvements in the history of humankind." AI is yet to deliver those incredible improvements. It has delivered deepfakes, huge quantities of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the permissionless resale of past intellectual labor, plus high energy and RAM prices. As well as some productivity gains in certain areas like coding, albeit at an unknown cost to future job markets. But as AI boosters insist, miracle drugs and endless vacations aren't far off … perhaps along with existential crises. Katharine Trendacosta, director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told The Register in an email that the EFF is glad to see state officials taking action against AI companies taking unreasonable risks with public safety. "Several recent cybersecurity incidents at AI labs could have been prevented or substantially mitigated by adhering to longstanding cybersecurity best practices, such as proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging," said Trendacosta. "AI agents can be useful tools when deployed appropriately, with adequate safeguards designed to mitigate the risks. Companies should carefully consider the risks of every use case, including the consequences, reversibility, and sensitivity of any action an agent is used for." ®

item.title: Pochettino: I’d tell Guardiola to ‘take it’ if he’s offered US coaching job
item.description: As he prepares to depart for Manchester United, the outgoing US coach held court on a number of topics, including what he’d change about soccer in America Outgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike. So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson. Continue reading...

item.title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
item.description: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. Read full article Comments

item.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
item.description: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates . Read full article Comments

item.title: Switzerland roll over sorry Scotland to increase the pressure on Pocognoli
item.description: A match that should have been about 103 was instead about four. Andy Robertson is due acclaim for becoming the most capped player in Scotland’s history but how the full-back will wish the moment had arrived in different circumstances. A second-string Switzerland team pulled Scotland apart, raising further and significant questions about the suitability of Sébastien Pocognoli to carry out the job his paymasters boldly entrusted him with. Scottish FA giddiness about Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke, a hugely successful leader of the national team, is looking increasingly ridiculous. “I don’t think you’ve got time in international football,” said Robertson as dust settled here. Ouch. Continue reading...

item.title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
item.description: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data. "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register . According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

item.title: California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking

The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
item.description: null On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there. (Image credit: SETI) Why it mattered The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute. "The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's." The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University . The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI. As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13. The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also b eamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Relive Starship's historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and 'Mechazilla' tower catch
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase. It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable. Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did. The 33 Raptor engines of SpaceX's Starship V3 rocket during its test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench. Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies. Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II , with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away. EOS R5 Mark II: $3999 This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling. Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review . View Deal Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas, as a bird passes on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space , while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase. Super Heavy (top) performs a boostback burn after stage separation as Ship 42 (bottom) fires its engines on its way to space. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase. Super Heavy descends back toward Texas on Nov.
item.dc:creator: Josh Dinner
item.content:encoded: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase. It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable. Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did. The 33 Raptor engines of SpaceX's Starship V3 rocket during its test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench. Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies. Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II , with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away. EOS R5 Mark II: $3999 This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling. Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review . View Deal Starship climbs the sky above Starbase, Texas, as a bird passes on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space , while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase. Super Heavy (top) performs a boostback burn after stage separation as Ship 42 (bottom) fires its engines on its way to space. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase. Super Heavy descends back toward Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Super Heavy flies back toward Texas, firing its engines to slow its descnet on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball. Super Heavy flies back toward Texas, firing its engines to slow its descnet on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system. Three-panel image showing Super Heavy's landing burn, engine cutoff and subsequent explosion. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) Ship continued on to low Earth orbit , where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites . It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation. Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch. SpaceX's Starship V3 rocket launches on a test flight from Starbase, Texas on May 22, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower. Starship upper stage approaches the launch tower in Starbase, Texas on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight. Starship upper stage lowers into the launch tower in Starbase, Texas on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) The six Raptor 3 engines that powered Ship 42's return are seen as the vehicle hangs by the arms of the "Mechazilla" launch tower arms. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry. Starship hangs, caught by its launch tower on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities. Starship hangs, caught by its launch tower on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner)

item.title: This Week’s Playlist Update Comes With Wande Coal, Seyi Shay, Olamide, Khaid & More
item.description: Seyi Shay teams up with French artist Vegedream on her new single “Love & War”, one of the standout releases in this week’s music roundup. Photo Credit: Instagram A fresh Monday means it is time to clear out last week’s queue and make room for the sounds shaping Nigerian music right now. From Wande Coal reuniting with Juls and Patoranking linking up with Olamide for a musical salute to Lagos, to Khaid bridging generations with Fuji legend Saheed Osupa , Spyro delivering a quick dancefloor starter, and Seyi Shay trading English and French verses with Vegedream , there is plenty to keep your headphones busy over the next few days. Wande Coal – “Kowope” Kicking things off is Wande Coal , who reunites with British-Ghanaian producer Juls on “Kowope”, marking their first collaboration since the hit “So Mi So”. The new single is also Wande Coal’s first solo release since he put out his 15-track album KING COAL in June. This time, the pair lean into warm, percussion-led Afropop, with lyrics centred on wealth,celebration and abundance. Ahead of its release on 12 November 2026, Wande Coal gave fans a taste of what was coming with a video staged as an owambe celebration inside a banking hall—a fitting preview for a song that takes its cues from the festive side of Nigerian life. ﻿ Patoranking featuring Olamide – “Welcome to Lagos” Keeping that celebratory mood going, Patoranking and Olamide join forces on “Welcome to Lagos” to give Nigeria’s commercial capital its own musical tribute. The Afro-dancehall collaboration captures the city’s familiar mix of hustle,nightlife and everyday movement, with both artists bringing their distinct sounds to the record. Patoranking opens with his dancehall delivery, setting the pace before Olamide takes over with Yoruba verses rooted in the city’s street culture.Released on 10 November 2026 alongside an official music video, the track gives two of Nigerian music’s established names a chance to celebrate the city that continues to inspire countless songs. ﻿ Khaid featuring King Dr. Saheed Osupa – “Yasin” Switching lanes from contemporary street anthems to a meeting of two musical eras, Khaid takes an unexpected turn on “Yasin” alongside Fuji veteran King Dr. Saheed Osupa . The song brings Khaid’s contemporary Afrobeats melodies together with Osupa’s traditional Fuji vocals and talking-drum rhythms, giving both artists room to draw on their distinct musical styles. An official lyric video followed on 14 November 2026. With this collaboration, Khaid steps beyond the sound audiences may be most familiar with, while Osupa brings his unmistakable Fuji influence to a new musical setting. ﻿ Spyro – “Kpan Kpan” If you are looking to pick up the tempo even further, Spyro keeps things firmly on the dancefloor with “Kpan Kpan”, a two-minute, 19-second Afropop release produced by Colonel Tyemmy . The track is built around bouncy percussion and a hook that is easy to pick up, making it a straightforward party selection. Released on 13 N

Released on 13 November 2026, “Kpan Kpan” keeps the arrangement brief and gets straight to its upbeat, dance-ready sound. ﻿ Seyi Shay featuring Vegedream – “Love & War” Slowing things down to close out the week’s roundup, Seyi Shay and French-Ivorian singer Vegedream explore the complicated side of romance on “Love & War”, a bilingual duet shaped like a conversation between two people after a breakup. Produced by Grammy-winning producer Harmony “ HMoney ” Samuels , the song moves between Seyi Shay’s English verses and Vegedream’s French vocals, with both artists approaching the relationship from their own perspectives. item.title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
item.description: Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week. The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Johana Bhuiyan
item.content:encoded: Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week. The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said. Continue reading...

item.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
item.description: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

item.title: Shareholders sue Intel, its CEO, and CFO after stock drops 28.6 percent in one day
item.description: Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel's stock on October 30. The lawsuit ( PDF ), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants. The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period. Read full article Comments

item.title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is just cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
item.description: AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast's cable broadband service and Wi-Fi are "fiber-powered." "This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide," AT&T's lawsuit said. "At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are 'Fiber-Powered.'" While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. Read full article Comments

item.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
item.description: null As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines." The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage. V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shared this chart depicting the evolution of SpaceX's Starship vehicles from the V2 to the planned V4 variant in August 2025. Exact specifications for Starship V4 are evolving. (Image credit: SpaceX/Elon Musk) Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9 , SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide. This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027. That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height." So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.
