item.content:encoded: null Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth. NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating." During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4. Going the distance Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2 . NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/KSC) A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet. Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s . The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did. Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan , executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane. An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return. NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said. Flying into the black Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Big Bang" because of its impact on the mission. "It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp." Voyager 1 officially entered interstellar space on Aug. 25, 2012. (Image credit: Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library/Getty Images) While the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes said their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here." The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes said, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going. Voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

item.title: Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet
item.description: Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Like most distros, Omaxian is available as an ISO file you can install and use. Alternatively, Omaxian Shell can be installed on an existing Debian-family distro without replacing the underlying operating system. The OS release is codenamed "Trans-Siberian Shaman," and the GitHub project repository shows work going back just a few weeks. No LLM coding assistant is credited on the project page, but we looked inside some of the test scripts, and as well as being verbose and hard to read, they also credit "Grok Bot." Omarchy itself is of course built with LLM assistance, and as we reported last month , so is the new Daemonarchy FreeBSD-based desktop project. Omaxian is styled after Omarchy, and it includes some of the same tools – and optional support for LLMs – but it's not based on the same tech. Instead of Arch, it's based on Devuan 6, the current version of the systemd-free fork of Debian. Omaxian eschews Hyprland, and indeed Wayland altogether: it opts for an X11 tiling window manager – in this case, i3 . i3 first appeared in 2009, so it's been around much longer than Hyprland. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win. The window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too. We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win. The window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too. We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. Xfce provides Omaxian with a file manager and other accessories, but you can just choose Xfce from the login screen and find yourself back in a simple, familiar, classic desktop environment. Omaxian is not the sort of environment we're looking for. This vulture isn't a developer and doesn't use LLMs for anything at all. However, lots of people are looking for something like that, as demonstrated by Omarchy's sponsorship . But it's bold, colorful, and significantly different from the mainstream, and that is the sort of thing we do like to see. ®

item.title: We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone
item.description: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. item.dc:creator: Rupert Goodwins
item.content:encoded: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. It is quite natural, when being bent over a barrel ceases to be an amusing pastime, to seek a less barrel-shaped position. In this case, the pressure to find alternatives has many elements. As well as the cost, support for Macs and Chromebooks becomes problematic. Both platforms are heavily represented in education at various levels, with the Macbook Neo thundering onto the battlefield with colors flying. Add to that the pressure towards digital sovereignty in Microsoft's own colonial outposts, the accelerants for an Old World version of the Boston Tea Party are only building. We even have a Boston of our very own . It's very nice. Microsoft isn't threatening anyone with guns and rapine, not yet anyway, and the whipping away of free student access to email and Teams only feels like extortion because of the misery it is causing across the sector. It is perfectly legal for Microsoft to cause as much suffering coated in balderdash as it likes. It is also perfectly legal to return the favor by actively seeking a sector-wide migration strategy. There are pioneers to learn from, especially huge multi-state, multi-supply chain organizations like Airbus and the various European governmental entities that are some way down that path already. This growing pool of expertise may be the most important factor in being able to react to Microsoft's efforts to turn education into a science fair experiment in high velocity frog boiling — one where the frog most definitely feels the heat — that and the growing distaste for the antics of American big tech. It's not just the forcing of unwanted technology that makes the barrel increasingly unbearable, nor using that as an excuse to charge more, it's what the companies are actually trying to do in Europe. Google Chromebooks are nice. Google wolves invading your villages because the company illegally erased their ecosystem are not nice. You thought those Wi-Fi snooping Maps cars were bad? The Microsoft educational platform "evolution" is foolhardy, counterproductive, and hugely tone deaf. It will not make it new lifetime customers, it will increase the speed at which its already hostile constituency grows resentment and appetite for radical action. Colonies revolt when the time is right, and empires are lost when arrogance and under-estimation of the situation combine with mismanagement and strategic blindness. The US midterms showed how that storm is blowing in. To choose this time to provoke an entire global sector is functional illiteracy writ large. Perhaps Microsoft should get an education. ®

item.title: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks
item.description: Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world. The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino . Continue reading...

item.title: Wunmi Adelusi: Why Are We Still Hiding That We Use AI?
item.description: Not long ago, I finished a piece of writing I was proud of — my thoughts, my argument, my structure. I had used an AI tool to help tighten the grammar and smooth the flow. And then, before sharing it, I went hunting through the text to delete every long dash. Why? Because the em dash has become the internet’s favourite “tell” that AI was involved. I was, quite literally, editing my work to hide a tool I had every right to use. When I caught myself doing it, I had to laugh. And then I had to ask: why the shame? It turns out I am not alone. Across a study spanning 47 countries, 57% of employees admit to concealing how they use AI at work. The reasons are almost entirely about reputation. In one recent survey of 5,000 desk workers, nearly half said they worried about appearing less capable or less competent, and a third feared they would simply look lazy. We are using the tools, and quietly scrubbing the fingerprints. There is even a quiet hypocrisy to it. Another survey says out of 7,200 adults, 46% said they would not disclose AI’s role in their own work while the remaining 54% said other people should. I had assumed this reticence was a particularly African trait. In my own experience, my colleagues in DC and Europe — my manager included — are refreshingly matter-of-fact about it. In one meeting recently, when asked to find a specific document in a shared folder, my manager cheerfully said he’d just let AI search it rather than disturb anyone’s work. Someone joked about his “secret agent,” and we all laughed. It was open, unbothered, upfront. I had concluded that we, of African descent, were simply more conservative, more inclined to glorify the heavy lifting, to wear “I stayed up all night doing it myself” as a badge of honour. But the research corrected me. This isn’t cultural; it’s universal. Employees across the US, UK, Europe, Latin America, Japan and Australia hide their AI use at strikingly similar rates. Even leadership does it. In some studies, managers conceal their AI use more than junior staff do. So perhaps the real question is why do we treat AI-assisted work as less credible than work done the hard way? I’ve even heard of recruiters downgrading CVs that look AI-generated, penalising the polish itself. But surely the more useful question is whether the substance behind it is real. A candidate who used a tool to sharpen how they present genuine experience hasn’t cheated; they’ve shown resourcefulness. The due diligence should be on verifying the claims, not on detecting the dashes. Screening out the tell, rather than testing the truth, risks rejecting capable people for the crime of being efficient. Because when you think about it, the logic is backwards. Using AI well is not a shortcut that replaces thinking; it is a skill that reveals it. You cannot get something excellent out of these tools without putting something substantial in. A vague mind produces vague prompts and vague results. Some of the people I am most impressed by at
item.dc:creator: Wunmi Adelusi
item.content:encoded: Not long ago, I finished a piece of writing I was proud of — my thoughts, my argument, my structure. I had used an AI tool to help tighten the grammar and smooth the flow. And then, before sharing it, I went hunting through the text to delete every long dash. Why? Because the em dash has become the internet’s favourite “tell” that AI was involved. I was, quite literally, editing my work to hide a tool I had every right to use. When I caught myself doing it, I had to laugh. And then I had to ask: why the shame? It turns out I am not alone. Across a study spanning 47 countries, 57% of employees admit to concealing how they use AI at work. The reasons are almost entirely about reputation. In one recent survey of 5,000 desk workers, nearly half said they worried about appearing less capable or less competent, and a third feared they would simply look lazy. We are using the tools, and quietly scrubbing the fingerprints. There is even a quiet hypocrisy to it. Another survey says out of 7,200 adults, 46% said they would not disclose AI’s role in their own work while the remaining 54% said other people should. I had assumed this reticence was a particularly African trait. In my own experience, my colleagues in DC and Europe — my manager included — are refreshingly matter-of-fact about it. In one meeting recently, when asked to find a specific document in a shared folder, my manager cheerfully said he’d just let AI search it rather than disturb anyone’s work. Someone joked about his “secret agent,” and we all laughed. It was open, unbothered, upfront. I had concluded that we, of African descent, were simply more conservative, more inclined to glorify the heavy lifting, to wear “I stayed up all night doing it myself” as a badge of honour. But the research corrected me. This isn’t cultural; it’s universal. Employees across the US, UK, Europe, Latin America, Japan and Australia hide their AI use at strikingly similar rates. Even leadership does it. In some studies, managers conceal their AI use more than junior staff do. So perhaps the real question is why do we treat AI-assisted work as less credible than work done the hard way? I’ve even heard of recruiters downgrading CVs that look AI-generated, penalising the polish itself. But surely the more useful question is whether the substance behind it is real. A candidate who used a tool to sharpen how they present genuine experience hasn’t cheated; they’ve shown resourcefulness. The due diligence should be on verifying the claims, not on detecting the dashes. Screening out the tell, rather than testing the truth, risks rejecting capable people for the crime of being efficient. Because when you think about it, the logic is backwards. Using AI well is not a shortcut that replaces thinking; it is a skill that reveals it. You cannot get something excellent out of these tools without putting something substantial in. A vague mind produces vague prompts and vague results. Some of the people I am most impressed by at work are often the ones who prompt AI brilliantly, who feed it sharp, well-framed inputs and get back something genuinely useful. That is not a sign they did less work, but that they thought clearly about what they wanted. So how do we move from hiding to owning? A few things I am learning to practise: Disclose simply, without apology. A lecturer in my doctoral programme put it well: “Even when you use AI only to refine, add a brief note that the ideas and perspectives are mine; AI assisted with structure, editing or grammar.” It isn’t an apology. It’s integrity. It marks clearly where your thinking ends, and the tool begins. Own the thinking, not just the output. The credibility of your work rests on the judgement behind it. Be able to explain your argument, defend your choices, and stand behind every claim, whether or not a tool helped you polish it. AI should sharpen your voice, not replace it. Use it to do more, not to do less. The goal isn’t to offload the work; it’s to free yourself for higher-value thinking. When AI handles the search, the first draft, the formatting, you have more room for the judgment only you can bring. Keep your discretion. Not every tool is safe for every input. Be thoughtful about what you feed into AI, confidential or proprietary information deserves real care. Owning your AI use also means using it responsibly. Finally, stop scrubbing the fingerprints. When I use AI to strengthen my work, I will say so, without feeling it makes me look less intelligent, less hardworking, or less capable. Because knowing how to use a powerful tool well, and being honest about it, is exactly the kind of judgement the future of work will reward. So tell me, what has your experience been? Do you own up to it, or quietly scrub the fingerprints too? *** Featured Image by PNW Production for Pexels. item.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
item.description: Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out. It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. item.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
item.description: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

item.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
item.description: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch. Continue reading...

item.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
item.description: Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s software The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it. As Guardian Australia reported in September , Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare. Continue reading...

item.title: 30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes
item.description: null You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026. The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully. In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!). Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars. So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can! (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) "Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena. Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996. While " Independence Day " saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure. (Image credit: Warner Bros Pictures) Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. item.content:encoded: null You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026. The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully. In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!). Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars. So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can! (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) "Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena. Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996. While " Independence Day " saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure. (Image credit: Warner Bros Pictures) Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result. Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs… Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam! (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status. Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly . "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.” It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got. (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory. MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks! Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them. (Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures) It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's " Disclosure Day " from a few months ago. In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet. This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka! "Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
item.description: null On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: The Macallan Unveils A Night on Earth: The First Light in Nigeria
item.description: The Macallan , the renowned single malt Scotch whisky, officially launched “A Night on Earth: The First Light in Nigeria” at an exclusive event held at the Radisson Blu, Victoria Island, Lagos. The launch introduced the fourth release in the brand’s limited-edition A Night on Earth series, with retail partners Booze.ng, Drinks.ng, Barrels and Naijaliquor and others supporting its presence in the Nigerian market ahead of the festive season. The launch brought the story behind The First Light to life, introducing guests to an expression inspired by the first sunrise of the New Year in New Zealand, one of the first places in the world to welcome the occasion. The release explores the anticipation of new beginnings and the significance of shared moments, themes that resonate with the festive season as people prepare to reconnect with loved ones, celebrate milestones and look ahead to the year to come. Guiding guests through the experience was Yinka Adepetu , The Macallan Brand Educator and Ambassador, who walked them through the inspiration, design and whisky-making craft behind the release. His presentation offered insight into the details that shape The First Light, from its connection to New Zealand’s New Year traditions to the choices behind its distinctive presentation and flavour profile. The fourth expression in the series carries its story through a three-layer gift box designed by New Zealand-born artist Bonnie Brown. The artwork captures the transition from dusk to dawn, with crimson bonfires, deep blue fireworks and the amber glow of first light. Together, these elements reflect the atmosphere of New Year celebrations and the anticipation that comes with a fresh start, making the presentation an integral part of the release’s identity. The whisky itself reflects The Macallan’s approach to cask selection and maturation. Matured in sherry-seasoned American and European oak casks, alongside casks that previously held bourbon, the expression presents notes of sweet oak, vanilla, caramelised marshmallows and a hint of Manuka honey on the nose. The palate develops with berry compote, rich caramel, vanilla ice cream and stone fruits, followed by a finish of gentle spice and mellow oak. Speaking on the launch, Hammed Adebiyi , Senior Brand Manager, West and Central Africa,Edrington Portfolio, said: “A Night on Earth: The First Light brings together the craftsmanshipthat defines The Macallan and a story that speaks to the significance of new beginnings. Inspired by the first sunrise of the New Year in New Zealand, this release celebrates the moments we share and the traditions we create with the people who matter to us. We are pleased to introduce this latest chapter of the series to Nigeria as the festive season approaches, a time when togetherness, reflection and thoughtful gifting take on particularmeaning.” With its Nigerian debut, A Night on Earth: The First Light extends The Macallan’s exploration of the relationship between whisky-making, ar

item.title: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar Makes History as First Female Vice-Chancellor of UNIJOS
item.description: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar, appointed as the 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor and first female Vice-Chancellor of the University of Jos. The University of Jos (UNIJOS) has officially appointed Professor Patricia Mamko Lar as its 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor, making her the first woman to occupy the position since the institution was established in 1971. Announced on Thursday, 12 November 2026 by the university’s Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of Council, Senator Grace Folashade Bent , during a special meeting of the 15th Governing Council, the historic appointment sees Professor Lar succeed Professor Tanko Ishaya as she takes the helm of the Plateau State institution. Born in Langtang, Plateau State, Professor Lar is a distinguished Professor of Medical Microbiology whose career has been deeply woven into the fabric of UNIJOS for nearly four decades. After earning her Bachelor of Science degree in Microbiology from Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria in 1986, she joined the University of Jos in 1987 as a Graduate Assistant in the Department of Medical Microbiology. She later went on to earn her Master’s degree in Medical Microbiology in 1989 and her PhD in Medical Parasitology in 1998 from the University of Lagos, followed by postdoctoral training at the Institute of Human Virology, University of Maryland in the United States under the NIH-Fogarty Fellowship Programme. Rising steadily through the academic ranks, she became an Associate Professor in 2012 before attaining full professorship in October 2015. Over the years, she has built an impressive body of work with more than 40 scholarly publications focusing on infectious diseases, including HIV/AIDS, malaria, antimicrobial resistance, and phytomedicine. Beyond the lecture hall and laboratory, Professor Lar has also served in key administrative roles at UNIJOS—including Head of the Department of Microbiology and Director of Linkages and Collaborations—and previously served a six-month tenure as Acting Vice-Chancellor of Yakubu Gowon University (formerly the University of Abuja) following her appointment by President Bola Tinubu in February 2025. Alongside her academic and leadership credentials, Professor Lar is a recognised advocate for women’s empowerment, having received the He4She Certificate of Award for Women Empowerment Activism in 2019. As she begins her five-year single term as UNIJOS’s first female substantive Vice-Chancellor after 55 years, she brings nearly four decades of institutional experience to the university’s top seat. The post Professor Patricia Mamko Lar Makes History as First Female Vice-Chancellor of UNIJOS appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
item.description: null For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle. Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare? "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued. Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth. An animation of T. CrB brightening. (Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab) "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold." Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event. "There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center , told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption." item.content:encoded: null For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle. Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare? "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued. Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth. An animation of T. CrB brightening. (Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab) "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold." Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event. "There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center , told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption." Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain." What will happen when T CrB's nova light reaches Earth? There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum. "The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude , then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer. Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day." The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky. "The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays , light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. " Where can I find the Blaze Star in the night sky? T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side. Corona Borealis forms a crown-like pattern of stars between the more famous constellations of Bootes and Hercules. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva) It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours. How to find T.CrB near Epsilon Coronae Borealis. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva) Want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky , along with our picks of the best cameras , lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

item.title: Duke’s Infant & Child Foundation Brings Experts Together to Empower Generation Next Leaders
item.description: The future of every society is sitting in our classrooms, growing up in our homes and navigating a world that is changing faster than ever before. But an important question confronts parents, educators and society: Are we truly preparing our children for the future, or are we simply raising them for the world we once knew? This is the conversation the Train The Trainers Summit (TTTS) Lagos Edition seeks to ignite when it convenes on Saturday, 28 November 2026, at the D’Podium International Event Centre, Aromire, Ikeja, off Adeniyi Jones, Lagos. Under the compelling theme, Empowering Our Generation Next Leaders: Raising Children to Thrive and Lead, the summit will bring together diverse experts, thought leaders, educators, parents and child development advocates for an important gathering focused on the future of children and the responsibilities of those raising them. Powered by Duke’s Infant & Child Foundation , the summit is built around a powerful conviction: children do not become confident, responsible and capable leaders by accident. They must be intentionally nurtured, properly guided, adequately protected and equipped with the skills and values required to navigate life. Today’s children are growing up in a world of artificial intelligence, digital exposure, changing social influences, emotional pressures, evolving relationships and unprecedented opportunities. While the world is changing, the responsibility of parents, teachers and other adults must also evolve. Speaking at the summit, the convener, Augusta Anyanwu- Egbom said “The question is no longer simply whether children are going to school. It is whether they are developing the emotional intelligence, resilience, critical thinking, digital awareness, identity, confidence and values needed to thrive beyond the classroom.” The Lagos Edition promises an engaging and insightful experience featuring diverse experts and speakers across parenting, education, technology, child psychology, social-emotional development, identity, safety, inclusion and other critical areas of child development. Participants can expect thought-provoking keynote conversations, fireside chats, practical demonstrations, interactive learning sessions and expert-led engagements addressing issues that families, schools and communities can no longer afford to ignore. From understanding the realities of modern parenting to navigating technology and digital safety; from protecting children against harmful influences to strengthening their emotional and social development, the summit will confront difficult questions and explore practical ways to create better outcomes for Generation Next. It will also challenge the traditional assumption that raising children is the responsibility of parents and teachers alone. A child’s development is shaped by an ecosystem involving families, schools, communities, institutions, technology, policy and society. If we want a generation that can lead tomorrow, we must prepare the adults

item.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
item.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. Continue reading...

item.title: Team Nigeria Records Its Best-Ever Youth Olympic Gold Medal Haul at Dakar 2026
item.description: Nigerian sprint champions Praise Tejiri Ugoh, Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo, and Gift Bright celebrate their historic gold medal victories at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps Team Nigeria delivered an unforgettable chapter at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal, wrapping up a historic multi-sport gathering that marked the first time an Olympic-branded event was ever hosted on African soil. Spanning across vibrant venues in Dakar, Diamniadio, and Saly, the Games brought together thousands of young athletes across 25 sports in a true celebration of youth culture, elite competition and unity. The grandeur of the international sporting festival kicked off with a breathtaking opening ceremony at the packed Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio. The night dazzled spectators with rich West African cultural displays, vibrant musical showcases, and a live performance by Nigerian music artist Ibquake , who brought incredible flair to the historic arena alongside global digital stars like Khaby Lame . Amidst the festive atmosphere, the Nigerian delegation walked with immense pride, led by sprint prodigy Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo carrying the national flag. Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo rejoices on the track wrapped in the green and white national flag after securing the women’s 100m gold. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps/Instagram When the action shifted to the tracks at the Complexe Iba Mar Diop, Team Nigeria turned the athletics arena into a showcase of pure speed, finishing their campaign with a total of three medals—all of them gold. Fifteen-year-old Gift Bright set the blazing pace by conquering the men’s 100m final in a personal-best and Games-record time of 10.28 seconds, earning the distinction of becoming the first Nigerian men’s 100m champion at the Youth Olympics. Gift Bright powers down the track en route to winning the men’s 100m gold in a personal-best 10.28 seconds. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps/Instagram Matching that stellar brilliance, flagbearer Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo blazed across the finish line in the women’s 100m final in 11.16 seconds, completing a phenomenal sprint double that crowned Nigeria as the first nation in Youth Olympic history to sweep both 100m titles at a single edition. The golden sweep was officially sealed by sixteen-year-old Praise Tejiri Ugoh , who stormed through the women’s 400m final in a personal-best time of 52.76 seconds to claim gold and become the first Nigerian to conquer the 400m distance at the Games. Praise Tejiri Ugoh claims gold for Nigeria on the podium following the women’s 400m final at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Photo Credit: MakingOfChamps/Instagram These remarkable achievements by Gift Bright, Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo, and Praise Tejiri Ugoh not only surpassed Nigeria’s previous best tally of two gold medals from the inaugural Singapore 2010 Games, but also firmly established the country’s rising track stars as global names to watch. item.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
item.description: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . item.content:encoded: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. Telling the tale of a dirty snowball Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space. Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten. "We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement . Comet 220P/McNaught imaged from an observatory in Spain on 7 August following its second outburst. (Image credit: Peter Carson.) While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere. A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes , which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home. The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter -family comet. "Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," said Trigo-Rodríguez. Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune . An illustration of a comet approaching Earth. (Image credit: Robert Lea) Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth . "Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids." For now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031. The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society .

item.title: New DStv Packages Arrive With A Bang At #ExpectMore Launch Event
item.description: On Wednesday, 4 November some of your favourite entertainment and lifestyle personalities converged at The Royal Box, Victoria Island, as MultiChoice Nigeria, a CANAL+ company, unveiled its new DStv and GOtv package line-up under the ‘Expect More’ campaign. The evening blended performances with a first-hand look at the new packages, had personalities including media executive Obi Asika , filmmaker Tola Odunsi , actors William Benson and Enado Odigie, entertainment power couple Darey and Deola Art-Alade , costume designer Yolanda Okereke, BBNaija stars Temi Nkem, Kola Omotosho and Imisi Ayanwale , and media personalities Uti Nwachukwu, Chuey Chu and Hero Daniels in attendance. Co-hosting the evening were media personality and actress Folu Storms and Deji Osikoya, who kept the energy high throughout, guiding guests through the night’s programme and the interactive spaces inspired by each package. Media Personalities Folu Storms And Deji Osikoya On The Red Carpet At The #ExpectMoreNaija Event Welcoming guests, MultiChoice Nigeria CEO Kemi Omotosho described the launch as the start of a new era for subscribers, with packages shaped by what Nigerians have asked for: more value, more choice and more content that speaks to them “We are in a new era of entertainment, and it is made for our customers,” she said. “From the 5th of November, we’re going to be doing three big things: giving you more choice and a clear, easy line-up, so you can choose what you want.” The Loud Urban Choir Performing at the #ExpectMoreNaija Event The night also featured a moving performance from spoken word artist Ibquake , while The Loud Urban Choir had the room singing along to a medley of some of Nigeria’s biggest songs. So, what’s new? Under the new structure, DStv packages now comprise Starter, Select, Sports and Premium, while GOtv customers can choose from Easy, Starter, Select and Sports. Starter (₦6,000) now includes two brand-new channels, SuperSport KICKOFF and Africa Magic+, bringing football and homegrown drama to more Nigerian homes. For the die-hard football fans, Sports (₦21,000) covers every Premier League and Champions League match, plus WWE and UFC. For more details, head over to www.dstv.com and www.gotvafrica.com , and join the conversation with #ExpectMoreOnDStv and #ExpectMoreNaija. item.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
item.description: As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup. There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Ewan Murray
item.content:encoded: As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup. There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution. Continue reading...
